## TL;DR

The Hub add-server form let unsafe addresses reach the network. `file:///…`, `ftp://…` and `http:/…` were rewritten into `https://` hosts named `file`, `ftp` or `http`, and then fetched, while the user saw a vague "Unreachable". I fixed the parser so only `https` gets through, tightened the health check so a plain web page can't be saved as a server, refused duplicate names, reworded every error to say what is wrong and what to do, announced errors to screen readers, and corrected the Android Hub docs, which wrongly said loopback HTTP works. A headless sweep of the fixtures at 360, 412, 768 and 1024 pixel widths passes 316 of 316 checks. This is browser evidence only; no device or real network was used.

## Work and rationale

The picker and add-server form live in `mobile/`, the Capacitor shell, not in the main web UI. I read `reachability.ts`, `app-state.ts`, `App.vue` and `AddServerView.vue`, and probed the form in headless Chromium with every network call routed to a mock.

The probe showed the real defects. The old `serverUrlOf` prepended `https://` to anything without an `http(s)://` prefix, so the scheme text became a host name. I replaced that with a parser that names the scheme and refuses it. `serverUrlProblem()` returns the plain-English reason, and `addServer` and `validateServer` both use it, so the form shows the same wording whether the problem is found before or after the network check.

The second defect came from the browser, not from my reading. Chromium's URL parser accepts `https://ok example` and produces the host `ok%20example`. Node's parser rejects it, so my first vitest run passed while the browser still sent a request. Native WebViews use WebKit or Chromium, so I now check the host and port text against an explicit character set before parsing.

The health check accepted any 2xx reply. The current handler returns `{ ok: true, … }`, so I now require that. A sign-in page or a plain website is refused with "isn't a RepoOS server". I did not check older RepoOS versions, and this rule is stricter than before.

Duplicate names were never checked, and the rename sheet closed even when a save was refused. `server-entries.ts` holds pure duplicate checks for the URL and the display name, case-insensitive, used by add and by rename. The sheet now shows the error inline. Duplicate checks run before the network, so a repeat never waits on a server.

The inline errors had no `role="alert"`, so a failed Save was silent for a screen reader. Both error paragraphs now have it.

The Android Hub user doc said loopback HTTP is supported. The code never allowed it, and the task requires refusing `http`. I corrected the doc instead of loosening the code.

I added `mobile/scripts/hub-picker-qa.ts`, a headless Playwright sweep against the `many` fixture. Every request goes through a route table: fixture hosts get canned replies and any other host is aborted. For addresses that should be refused before the network, the sweep asserts zero requests. I also wrote `docs/qa/2026-11-hub-picker-qa.md`, which records the method, the cases and what was not covered. It is left uncommitted for RepoOS to commit.

## Approaches tried

I first considered loosening the parser to allow `http://localhost`, since the docs asked for it. I dropped that. The task requires refusing `http`, and correcting the doc matched the code the team already shipped.

For the QA, I first asserted messages from the fixture alone. The first full sweep flagged the malformed-host case as a 10-second timeout message. A single-case probe showed the real request going to `ok%20example`. The sweep also read a stale error once. So the sweep now waits for the previous error to clear before reading the next one, and checks that it did.

I considered gating the QA script in `repoos check`. I kept it a script, because it needs a running Vite server and a browser, and the existing mobile fixture sweep is also a script.

## Challenges and blockers

`mobile/` had no `node_modules` in this worktree. `bun install` inside `mobile/` installed the declared dependencies, and `vue-tsc --noEmit` then passed.

The background Vite server was stopped by its own time limit after the sweep finished. That does not affect the recorded results.

The first `repoos check` run was cut off by my own 590-second command timeout, during the build step. The remote validation had already passed on the thinkpad host. I reran the check in the background with a longer limit.

A design question remains for a human. When two tailnet-discovered servers share a project name, the second add now fails with the duplicate-name message, and the user cannot rename it inside discovery. I did not change the discovery screen.

## Key learnings

A URL parser is not a single contract. The same string gave different results in Node and in Chromium, so tests that run only in Node can pass for a bug that ships. Fixture QA in a real browser caught what unit tests missed, and the check now lives in the sweep too.

Copy reviews need the rules as well as the strings. Each message changed only when the rule behind it was correct. The scheme message names the scheme, the query-string message names the characters to remove, and the health message names the reason, because the rule and the words had to agree.

Reading an error from a previous step is an easy mistake in browser tests. Waiting for the old error to clear, and checking that it did, removed the false results.

Evidence limits: the sweep covers Chromium at four widths with mocked replies. It does not cover a real device, a native WebView, touch, the on-screen keyboard, the Android back gesture, or a real network. Those still need a human device pass.
